United Kingdom.answer: For Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales), GOV.UK says you cannot bring meat, meat products, milk or dairy from outside the EU, with a few exceptions such as up to 2kg of powdered infant milk. From the EU, Switzerland, Norway and a few other places fish, poultry and eggs are allowed but most meat and all dairy are not. Undeclared banned products can mean a fine of up to £5,000 or prosecution.
sources: https://www.gov.uk/bringing-food-into-great-britain
GOV.UK — Bringing food into Great Britain
faq: Can I bring cheese or milk into Great Britain?

GOV.UK says no for dairy such as cheese, milk, butter and yoghurt, from the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, the Faroe Islands and Greenland as well as from other countries. The exception is up to 2kg of powdered infant milk, infant food or special medical food.
Can I bring meat into Great Britain?
Not from outside the EU. From the EU and the other listed places, pork, beef, lamb, mutton, goat, venison and products made from them, such as sausages, are not allowed, but poultry is.
Can I bring fruit and vegetables into Great Britain?

From the EU, Switzerland or Liechtenstein, yes for personal use. From other countries most need a phytosanitary certificate; without one you can bring only the items GOV.UK lists, such as pineapple, citrus fruit, banana, mango, dates and guava.
What happens if I do not declare banned food?
Border Force destroys declared banned products. If you do not declare them, GOV.UK says you could be fined up to £5,000 (in England) or prosecuted.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat and dairy from outside the EU are banned; from the EU, cheese, milk and most meat are banned too.

lines: You cannot bring meat or meat products, or milk or milk-based products.
Exceptions: up to 2kg per person of powdered infant milk, infant food or special food needed for medical reasons, in branded unopened packaging and not needing refrigeration.

scen.when: From the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, the Faroe Islands or Greenland
lines: No pork, beef, lamb, mutton, goat, venison or products made from them, such as sausages.
No cheese, milk, butter or yoghurt.
Poultry and its products, and other animal products such as eggs and honey, are allowed for personal use.

topics.label: Fish & seafood
topics.head: From outside the EU you can bring up to 20 kg of fish in total.

lines: Up to 20kg per person in total of fresh fish (gutted), fish products, processed fish (dried, cooked, cured or smoked), lobsters and prawns.
Up to 2kg per person of honey, live mussels or oysters, snails, frogs’ legs and insect protein.
Caviar needs a CITES permit.

topics.label: Fruit, veg & nuts
topics.head: Free from the EU; from elsewhere most need a plant health certificate.

scen.when: From the EU, Switzerland or Liechtenstein
lines: Fruit, vegetables, nuts and seeds are allowed for personal use.
Most fruit and vegetables need a phytosanitary certificate from the authorities of the country you leave.
Without one you may bring only pineapple, kiwi, coconut, citrus fruits, kumquat, persimmon, durian, curry leaves, banana and plantain, mango, dates, passion fruit and guava.
Processed and packaged plant products, peeled and processed nuts or nut butters, and certain grains such as rice are also allowed.

topics.label: Packaged food
topics.head: Bread, biscuits, pasta and similar items can come from any country.

lines: Bread (not sandwiches filled with meat or dairy), cakes without fresh cream, biscuits, chocolate and confectionery (not with a lot of unprocessed dairy), pasta and noodles (not meat-filled), packaged soup, stocks and flavourings.
Processed and packaged plant products, and food supplements with small amounts of an animal product such as fish oil capsules.

topics.label: Pet food
topics.head: Pet food is mostly banned from outside the EU; 2 kg only for health reasons.

scen.when: From the EU and the other listed places
lines: Pet food with pig, cow, sheep, goat or deer meat or animal products is not allowed.
Other pet food, such as chicken, is allowed if commercially packaged with the maker’s name and address, up to 2kg per person.
Not allowed unless your pet needs it for health reasons, then up to 2kg per person, unopened and branded, not needing refrigeration.
Your pet must travel with you and you should carry evidence such as a vet’s letter. For more than 2kg, email imports@apha.gov.uk.

topics.label: If you break the rules
topics.head: Banned items are destroyed; undeclared ones can mean a fine of up to £5,000.

lines: Declared banned products are taken away and destroyed by Border Force.
If you do not declare them, you could be fined up to £5,000 (in England) or prosecuted.
Border Force can also seize products that are cross-contaminated, for example with meat blood; contaminated clothing or bags are destroyed. You can appeal if you think products were wrongly seized.
Northern Ireland has different rules, which this page does not cover.

Canada.answer: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says you must declare all food products you bring into Canada, and most foods are capped at 20 kg (or 20 L for liquids) for personal use. Rules differ by origin: meat from the US is allowed if retail packaged, while from other countries only commercially prepared, cooked, shelf-stable meat in sealed containers is allowed. Eggs from outside the US are not permitted.
sources: https://inspection.canada.ca/en/food-safety-consumers/bring-food-personal-use
Canadian Food Inspection Agency — Bring food into Canada for personal use
faq: Do I have to declare food when entering Canada?
Yes. The CFIA says that when travelling you must declare all food products you bring with you, and the Canada Border Services Agency may inspect them at the point of entry.
How much food can I bring into Canada?

For personal use only, with caps such as 20 kg for meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables, 5 dozen eggs from the US, 50 L of non-alcoholic drinks and 50 L of food-grade oils. Most other foods are capped at 20 kg, or 20 L for liquids.
Can I bring meat into Canada?

From the US, retail packaged or labelled meat with proof of origin, up to 20 kg. From other countries, fresh, dried and cured meats such as ham and sausage are not permitted; only commercially prepared, cooked, shelf-stable products in sealed containers, up to 20 kg.
Can I bring eggs into Canada?
Retail-packaged eggs labelled Product of the USA, up to 5 dozen, from the US. Eggs from other countries are not permitted.

topics.label: Meat
topics.head: From the US retail-packaged meat is allowed; from elsewhere only cooked, sealed products.

lines: Only if you bring it with you, not by mail or courier, retail packaged or labelled, with proof of country of origin.
Farm or backyard meat that is not retail packaged is not permitted. Limit: 20 kg (44.09 lbs).
Fresh, dried and cured meats such as hams and sausages are not permitted.
Only commercially prepared, cooked, shelf-stable products in sealed containers, brought with you, up to 20 kg. Beef only from countries of negligible BSE risk.

topics.label: Dairy
topics.head: Up to 20 kg or 20 L; from outside the US only certain dairy products.

lines: No specific restrictions are listed for cheese, yogurt, butter, milk, ice cream and kashk.
Limit: 20 kg (44.09 lbs) or 20 L (5.28 US gal).
Only ice cream, yogurt, kashk and pasteurized cheese are permitted from any country.
Unpasteurized cheese only from countries free of certain animal diseases. Limit 20 kg or 20 L.

topics.label: Eggs
topics.head: Retail-packaged eggs from the US only, up to 5 dozen.

lines: Must be retail packaged, for human consumption, and labelled Product of the USA. Farm or backyard eggs are not permitted.
Processed egg products: up to 20 kg or 20 L.
Eggs are not permitted.

topics.label: Fruit & veg
topics.head: Up to 20 kg each; fresh produce from outside the US may be restricted.

lines: Fresh produce is subject to the Automated Import Reference System (AIRS).
Potatoes must be commercially packaged and graded US No.1. Limits: fruits 20 kg, vegetables 20 kg.
Fresh produce is subject to AIRS and may be restricted or prohibited depending on the country of origin; if permitted, 20 kg of fruit and 20 kg of vegetables.
Processed produce: 20 kg or 20 L.

topics.label: Drinks, oils & others
topics.head: Most other foods are fine within the quantity caps.

lines: Non-alcoholic beverages 50 L, food-grade oils 50 L, maple syrup 20 L, maple products 4 kg.
Most other foods, such as baked goods, confectionery, honey, spices, tea, coffee and grain foods: 20 kg, or 20 L for liquids.
Duties and taxes may apply above the personal exemption limits.
Alcohol and tobacco follow Canada Border Services Agency limits, which this page links to.

Japan.answer: Japan's Animal Quarantine Service requires every traveller bringing in meat, organs, eggs or processed products such as jerky, ham, sausages and bacon to be inspected at the counter in the baggage claim area, and these items need a government inspection certificate from the exporting country. Without one they cannot enter, even as souvenirs. Bringing them in illegally is punishable by up to 3 years in prison or a fine of up to 3 million yen.
sources: https://www.maff.go.jp/aqs/english/product/import.html
MAFF Animal Quarantine Service — importing animal products
faq: Can I bring meat or sausages into Japan?

Meat, organs and processed products such as jerky, ham, sausages and bacon need a government-issued inspection certificate from the exporting country. Without one they cannot be brought in, even as souvenirs or for personal use.
Can I bring eggs into Japan?
Eggs, including eggshells, are subject to animal quarantine and need the same inspection certificate.
Do I have to go through inspection when I arrive in Japan?
Yes: travellers must undergo import inspection at the Animal Quarantine Service counter in the baggage claim area of the arrival airport or seaport.
What is the penalty for bringing animal products into Japan illegally?
A custodial sentence of up to 3 years or a fine of up to 3 million yen (up to 50 million yen for businesses). The fine maximum was raised from 1 million yen on 1 July 2020.

topics.label: Meat & sausage
topics.head: Meat and processed meat need a government certificate from the exporting country.

lines: Meat, organs, eggs (including eggshells) and processed products are subject to quarantine. Examples named: jerky, ham, sausages, bacon and meat buns.
Items need a government-issued inspection certificate from the exporting country; without one they cannot be brought in, even as souvenirs or for personal use.
Vacuum-sealed, heat-processed, duty-free and small personal quantities are still not allowed if they are banned or lack a certificate.

topics.label: Eggs
topics.head: Eggs, shells included, are subject to animal quarantine.

lines: Eggs, including eggshells, need the same government inspection certificate.
Items from countries or regions with suspended imports cannot be brought in.

topics.label: Dried fish
topics.head: Dried fish without livestock meat or eggs is not subject to inspection.

lines: Dried fish without livestock meat or eggs is not subject to inspection, but an officer may check it on arrival.

topics.label: Fruit & veg
topics.head: The page states fruits and vegetables are illegal to bring in.

lines: The animal quarantine page states that bringing in fruits, vegetables and similar items is illegal, and links to a separate plant quarantine page that we did not read.
Check the plant protection pages of MAFF before you travel with any plant product.

topics.label: Inspection & fines
topics.head: You are inspected at the Animal Quarantine counter; breaking the rules can mean prison.

lines: Travellers must undergo import inspection at the Animal Quarantine Service counter in the baggage claim area, and officers can ask whether you carry animal products and inspect your luggage.
Bringing in meat or animal products illegally is punishable by a custodial sentence of up to 3 years or a fine of up to 3 million yen.
Failing to declare meat or animal products found in your luggage is also punishable, and officers may dispose of them.

United States.answer: USDA APHIS says every traveller entering the United States must declare all agricultural and wildlife products to U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and that if you declare everything you face no penalties even when an item cannot enter. Almost all fresh and frozen fruits and vegetables are prohibited, meat depends on the animal diseases in the country it comes from (50 pounds is the limit per item), and butter and solid cheeses may enter from any country.
sources: https://www.aphis.usda.gov/traveling-with-ag-products/another-country
USDA APHIS — Traveling from another country with food or agricultural products
https://www.aphis.usda.gov/traveling-with-ag-products/fruits-vegetables
USDA APHIS — International traveler: fruits and vegetables
https://www.aphis.usda.gov/traveling-with-ag-products/milk-dairy-eggs
USDA APHIS — International traveler: milk, dairy and egg products
faq: Do I have to declare food when entering the United States?

Yes. APHIS says travellers must declare all agricultural or wildlife products to CBP, and must also say if they visited a farm or touched animals before the trip. As long as you declare everything you will not face any penalties, even if an inspector decides an item cannot enter.
Can I bring fresh fruit and vegetables into the United States?

Almost all fresh and frozen fruits and vegetables, whole or cut, are prohibited, including ones given to you on a plane or cruise ship. Commercially canned ones are allowed if declared; home-canned products are not.
Can I bring cheese and butter into the United States?
Butter, butter oil and solid hard or soft cheeses may enter from any country if the cheese has no meat and does not pour like a liquid, such as ricotta or cottage cheese.
How much meat can I bring into the United States?

From countries without certain livestock diseases, with proof of origin, no more than 50 pounds of an item. Cured hams and salami from France, Germany, Italy and Spain may not be brought in by travellers.

topics.label: Declare it
topics.head: Declare all agricultural products; declared items bring no penalty even if refused.

lines: Travellers must declare all agricultural and wildlife products to CBP, and tell them if they visited a farm or were in contact with animals.
Inspectors have the final say. Keep receipts and original packaging as proof of the country of origin.
As long as you declare everything you will not face any penalties, even if an inspector decides the items cannot enter.

topics.label: Fruit & veg
topics.head: Almost all fresh and frozen fruit and vegetables are prohibited.

lines: Almost all fresh and frozen fruits and vegetables, whole or cut, are prohibited, including those given to you on an airplane or cruise ship. Plan to leave them behind.
Commercially canned fruit and vegetables are allowed if declared on your customs form; home-canned products are not.
Most dried fruit and vegetables are not allowed. Generally allowed if declared: beans, dates, figs, nuts (not chestnuts or acorns), okra, peas, raisins and Szechwan peppercorns.

topics.label: Meat & poultry
topics.head: Allowed from disease-free countries with proof of origin, up to 50 pounds of an item.

lines: Most is not allowed from countries with foot-and-mouth disease, BSE, swine vesicular disease, classical swine fever or African swine fever.
From countries without these diseases, fresh, cooked, cured or dried meat is allowed with proof of origin such as a label, receipt, passport or flight origin. Not more than 50 pounds of an item.
Cured hams (prosciutto, Serrano, Iberian) and salami from France, Germany, Italy and Spain may not be brought in by travellers.
Most poultry is not allowed from countries with highly pathogenic avian influenza or Newcastle disease.
Commercially packaged, cooked, shelf-stable poultry in unopened packages from affected countries is allowed, up to 50 pounds per item.

topics.label: Dairy & eggs
topics.head: Butter and solid cheeses are allowed from any country; other dairy and eggs depend on origin.

lines: Most milk and dairy from countries with foot-and-mouth disease is not allowed, except small quantities of infant liquid milk and formula, and commercially packaged, cooked, shelf-stable finished foods.
Butter, butter oil and solid hard or soft cheese (no meat, and not pourable like ricotta) may enter from any country.
Most eggs and egg products from countries with avian influenza or Newcastle disease are not allowed.
From other countries, eggs are allowed with proof of origin. Clean decorated eggshells without egg white or yolk: up to 12 per person.

topics.label: Seafood
topics.head: APHIS does not regulate most seafood; other agencies do.

lines: APHIS only regulates breaded seafood whose breading contains milk or eggs.
For other seafood contact the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service or the Food and Drug Administration, whose numbers are on the page.

New Zealand.answer: The Ministry for Primary Industries says you must declare all food, animal products, plants and other risk goods on your New Zealand Traveller Declaration, and that any food, cooked, uncooked, fresh, preserved, packaged or dried, counts as a risk good. Failing to declare is a strict liability offence with a NZD$400 instant fine, and deliberate smuggling can mean up to NZD$100,000 and 5 years in prison.
sources: https://www.mpi.govt.nz/bring-send-to-nz/bringing-and-posting-items-to-nz/how-to-declare-items-when-arriving-in-nz/
Ministry for Primary Industries — How to declare items when arriving in NZ
https://www.mpi.govt.nz/bring-send-to-nz/bringing-and-posting-items-to-nz/what-happens-if-you-fail-to-declare
Ministry for Primary Industries — What happens if you fail to declare
faq: Do I have to declare all food in New Zealand?

Yes. MPI says to declare all food, animal products, plants and other specific items on your New Zealand Traveller Declaration (NZTD), free online or in the app. It counts any food, cooked, uncooked, fresh, preserved, packaged or dried, as a risk good.
What if I forget to declare something?
It is still an offence. MPI calls it a strict liability offence, even if you forgot or did not know the rules. The penalty is a NZD$400 infringement fee, with no criminal conviction.
What is the penalty for deliberate smuggling?
If you are convicted of deliberate smuggling you could be fined up to NZD$100,000 and sentenced to up to 5 years in prison.
Can I throw food away instead of declaring it?
MPI says you can dispose of undeclared risk goods in the marked amnesty bins on arrival, to avoid being searched or fined.

topics.label: Declare it
topics.head: Declare all food and animal or plant products; there is no excuse for forgetting.

scen.when: On the New Zealand Traveller Declaration
lines: Declare all risk goods like food, plants, wooden products, soil, water, outdoor equipment and animal products, even if you have nothing in your bags to declare you must still complete the declaration.
Declared items may be inspected. Dispose of undeclared risk goods in the marked amnesty bins on arrival to avoid being searched or fined.

topics.label: Any food
topics.head: MPI treats any food, cooked, fresh, packaged or dried, as a risk good.

lines: Any food: cooked, uncooked, fresh, preserved, packaged or dried.
Animals or animal products: meat, dairy products, fish, honey, bee products, eggs, feathers, shells, raw wool, skins, bones or insects.
Plants or plant products: fruit, flowers, seeds, bulbs, wood, bark, leaves, nuts, vegetables, fungi, cane, bamboo or straw, including for religious offerings or medicinal use.
MPI says it cannot list every risk good, because risk depends on the country, ingredients and packaging.
Use its Check if you can bring or send an item to NZ tool for specific foods and weight limits; we did not read that tool.

topics.label: Outdoor gear
topics.head: Items used outdoors or on farms must be declared too.

lines: Equipment used with animals, plants or water, and items used for outdoor or farming activities, including footwear, tents, camping, hunting, hiking, golf or sports equipment.
Other risk items include animal medicines, herbal medicines, biological cultures, organisms, soil and water.

topics.label: Fines
topics.head: Forgetting is no excuse: NZD$400 instant fine, up to NZD$100,000 for smuggling.

lines: The penalty for a false declaration is an NZD$400 infringement fee, an instant fine, with no criminal conviction. It applies even if you forgot, were careless or did not know the rules or what was in your baggage.
You can pay within 14 days, ask for a waiver, or request a court hearing.
If you deliberately make an incorrect or false declaration to conceal items and are convicted of smuggling, you could be fined up to NZD$100,000 and sentenced to up to 5 years in prison.

Australia.answer: Australia's Department of Agriculture says that by law you must declare if you are carrying certain food, plant material or animal products when you travel to Australia, and that goods are assessed by a biosecurity officer and may be inspected. Its list of foods to check covers items such as meat, dairy, eggs, rice, honey, nuts and fruit preserves, with detailed conditions in its BICON system. Footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas must be cleaned and declared.
sources: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/travelling/bringing-mailing-goods
Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Bringing or mailing goods to Australia
faq: Do I have to declare food when I arrive in Australia?

Yes. The department says that by law you must declare if you are carrying certain food, plant material or animal products. You can take declared goods to the clearance point for assessment, or voluntarily dispose of them in the terminal bins.
Where do I find the detailed rules for each food in Australia?

In the department's Biosecurity Import Conditions system (BICON). Its food and drink list covers items such as meat, cheese and dairy, eggs, honey, rice, nuts, noodles, spices, pet food and infant formula, but it says the list is not exhaustive.
What if my shoes or equipment were used on a farm?
All footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas or near animals must be thoroughly cleaned and declared on arrival.
What happens to goods that do not meet the import conditions?
They will be directed for treatment or exported at the importer's expense, or the traveller can voluntarily dispose of them.

topics.label: Declare it
topics.head: You must declare certain food, plant material and animal products.

lines: By law you must declare if you are carrying certain food, plant material or animal products.
You can take declared goods to the clearance point, where a biosecurity officer assesses them and they may be inspected. Or you can voluntarily dispose of them in the bins in the terminal.

topics.label: Food on the list
topics.head: The department lists food types to check before you travel.

lines: Biscuits, bread, cakes and pastries; cheese, butter and dairy; chocolate; coffee; fish; honey; infant formula; juice; meat items; noodles and pasta; nuts; oil; preserved fruit and vegetables; rice; sauces; seafood; spices; tea; wheat; whole eggs and more.
The page says the list is not exhaustive, and the conditions for each item are in the Biosecurity Import Conditions system (BICON), which we did not read.

topics.label: Farm items
topics.head: Footwear, clothing and equipment used on farms must be cleaned and declared.

lines: All footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas or near animals must be thoroughly cleaned and declared on arrival.

topics.label: Mail & rejected goods
topics.head: Mailed goods must be described accurately; goods that fail conditions are treated or exported.

scen.when: Goods that do not meet the conditions
lines: Goods that do not meet import conditions will be directed for treatment or exported at the importer’s expense, or you can voluntarily dispose of them.
Goods sent by mail must be accurately described on the postal declaration label.
We did not read the penalty amounts for failing to declare; check the department’s page on penalties before you travel.

Hong Kong.answer: Hong Kong's Imported Game, Meat, Poultry and Eggs Regulations require every consignment of game, meat, poultry and eggs, whether for personal use or not, to carry a health certificate or written permission from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department. Breaking the rule is punishable by a fine of HK$50,000 and 6 months in prison, and the Centre for Food Safety had brought 774 prosecutions against inbound travellers by 20 June 2024.
sources: https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202406/21/P2024062100547.htm
Hong Kong Government (Customs and Centre for Food Safety) — joint operation against illegal import of regulated food
faq: Can I bring meat, poultry or eggs into Hong Kong?
Only with a health certificate from the place of origin or written permission from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department. The law applies whether the food is for personal use or not.
What is the penalty for bringing regulated food into Hong Kong illegally?
On conviction, a maximum fine of HK$50,000 and six months' imprisonment under Cap. 132AK.
Does food from the Mainland need papers?
Yes: food from the Mainland needs a health certificate from Mainland Customs showing it comes from a registered plant recognised by the Mainland authority.
How common are prosecutions?
The Centre for Food Safety had brought 774 prosecutions against inbound persons for illegally bringing game, meat, poultry and eggs by 20 June 2024.

topics.label: Meat, poultry, game
topics.head: Every consignment needs a health certificate or written permission, even for personal use.

lines: Each consignment must be accompanied by a health certificate from the issuing entity of the place of origin, or by written permission from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD).

The rule applies whether the food is for personal use or not. Food from the Mainland needs a health certificate from Mainland Customs showing it is from a registered plant recognised for supplying Hong Kong.

topics.label: Eggs
topics.head: Eggs are regulated food with the same health certificate rule.

lines: The release names raw meat, poultry and eggs as its examples of illegal imports of regulated food.
Importing regulated food needs a recognised health certificate, FEHD written permission, or an import licence.

topics.label: Penalty
topics.head: A fine of HK$50,000 and six months in prison on conviction.

lines: Maximum penalty on conviction is a fine of $50,000 and six months’ imprisonment under Cap. 132AK.

Between 18 and 21 June 2024 a joint operation at Lo Wu, Lok Ma Chau Spur Line, Shenzhen Bay and Heung Yuen Wai found 15 cases; by 20 June the Centre for Food Safety had instituted 774 prosecutions that year.
The public can report suspected smuggling to the Customs 24-hour hotline, 2545 6182, or to crimereport@customs.gov.hk.

topics.label: Not read
topics.head: The release does not list other foods such as fruit or dairy.

lines: This government release covers regulated food: game, meat, poultry and eggs. It does not list rules for fruit, vegetables, dairy or packaged food, so check the Centre for Food Safety (cfs.gov.hk) before you bring them.

Germany.answer: Germany's Federal Ministry of Food says it is prohibited as a matter of principle to bring meat, milk and products derived from them into the EU from non-EU countries. Small amounts are allowed: up to 2 kg of infant milk, baby food and medically required food, up to 2 kg of other animal products such as honey, and up to 20 kg of fish. Goods that do not comply must go to a veterinary border inspection post or be surrendered on arrival.
sources: https://www.bmleh.de/EN/topics/consumer-protection/food-hygiene-safety/importation-products-animal-origin.html
Federal Ministry of Food (BMLEH) — Importation of products of animal origin for personal consumption
faq: Can I bring meat or cheese into Germany from a non-EU country?
No, as a matter of principle. The ministry says it is prohibited to bring meat, milk and products derived from them into the EU, with the exceptions listed on its page.
How much fish and honey can I bring into Germany?
Up to 20 kg of fish and fishery products, or one fish that may be heavier, and up to 2 kg of other animal products such as honey.
Is bread or chocolate allowed?

Yes, with no quantity limit: bread, cake, cookies, chocolate and confectionery, unless mixed or filled with meat. Pasta and noodles, pre-packaged supplements and soup aromas are also listed without limits.
What happens to goods that do not comply?

They must be presented to a veterinary border inspection post for import controls, or surrendered on arrival in the EU for official disposal at the importer's expense. Failing to register such products may result in a fine, but the page gives no amount.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat, milk and their products from non-EU countries are banned as a principle.

lines: It is prohibited as a matter of principle to bring meat, milk and products derived from them into the EU.
The rules do not apply to personal imports of animal products from Andorra, Liechtenstein, San Marino or Switzerland.
Larger personal amounts are allowed, from 10 to 20 kg depending on the product category.
Meat, milk and their derivatives are capped at 10 kg combined per person.

topics.label: Fish & honey
topics.head: Up to 20 kg of fish and 2 kg of other animal products such as honey.

lines: Fish and fishery products: up to 20 kg, or one single fish that may be heavier.
Other animal products, such as honey: up to 2 kg.
Fishery products for personal use from the Faroe Islands or Iceland are exempt from the limit.

topics.label: Baby & medical food
topics.head: Infant milk, baby food and medically required food are allowed up to 2 kg.

lines: Powdered infant milk, baby food and medically necessary special food: maximum 2 kg.
Medically necessary special pet food: maximum 2 kg.

topics.label: Foods with no limit
topics.head: Bread, biscuits, chocolate and pasta come in without a quantity limit.

lines: Bread, cake, cookies, chocolate and confectionery, unless mixed or filled with meat.
Pasta and noodles unless mixed or filled with meat, pre-packaged dietary supplements, meat extracts and concentrates, fish-filled olives, and pre-packaged consommé and soup aromas.
Other foods containing no fresh or processed meat, milk or dairy and less than 50% egg or fish products.

topics.label: If it does not comply
topics.head: Show it at a veterinary border post or surrender it for disposal.

lines: They must be presented to a veterinary border inspection post for import controls, or surrendered on arrival in the EU for official disposal at the importer’s expense.
Failing to register such products may result in a fine; the page does not give an amount.

France.answer: French Customs says meat and dairy products, and products made from them, are banned from most non-EU countries, with small exceptions for personal baggage and small parcels. Fish is allowed up to 20 kg, and powdered infant milk, medical food and other animal products such as honey up to 2 kg. If you exceed the limits or carry banned products, customs seizes and systematically destroys the goods.
sources: https://www.douane.gouv.fr/particuliers/vous-voyagez/denrees-alimentaires
French Customs (Douane) — Food products when you travel
faq: Can I bring meat or cheese into France from outside the EU?
No: customs says meat, milk and their products are banned from most non-EU countries. From the Faroe Islands and Greenland you may bring up to 10 kg combined.
What can I bring into France in small quantities?
Fish up to 20 kg, powdered infant milk, infant food and medically required food up to 2 kg, and other animal products such as honey or snails up to 2 kg per person.
Do I have to declare these products to French Customs?
Yes. Travellers must declare these products to customs and present them.
What does French Customs do with banned or excess food?
It seizes and systematically destroys the goods. Above the limits, postal and express freight clearance is not allowed.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat, milk and their products are banned from most non-EU countries.

lines: Meat, milk, and meat- or milk-based products are banned.
If you carry them, customs seizes and systematically destroys the goods.

scen.when: From the Faroe Islands or Greenland
lines: Meat, milk and their products: up to 10 kg per traveller, combined.

scen.when: From Andorra, Iceland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, Liechtenstein or Northern Ireland
lines: Travellers from these places can bring animal-origin foods with no quantity limit.

topics.label: Fish
topics.head: Up to 20 kg of fresh, prepared or processed fish; unlimited from the Faroe Islands and Greenland.

lines: Fresh, gutted, prepared or processed fish: up to 20 kg per person from most non-EU countries.
From the Faroe Islands and Greenland the amount is unlimited.

topics.label: Infant, medical & other
topics.head: Powdered infant milk, medical food and other animal products such as honey: up to 2 kg.

lines: Powdered infant milk, infant food and medically required special food: up to 2 kg (10 kg from the Faroe Islands and Greenland).
Medically required pet food, and other animal products such as honey or snails: up to 2 kg.

topics.label: Declare & fines
topics.head: You must declare and present these products to customs.

lines: Travellers must declare these products to customs and present them. For postal or express imports within the limits the declaration needs tariff provision Y058.
Above the thresholds, postal or express clearance is not allowed; larger amounts must go through commercial freight.
The page covers animal-origin products only; it says nothing about fruit, vegetables or plants, and describes no fines beyond seizure and destruction.

Ireland.answer: The Food Safety Authority of Ireland says meat and milk products are not allowed from third countries other than the Faroe Islands and Greenland, where up to 10 kg combined is allowed. Powdered infant milk and special medical food are allowed up to 2 kg, fish up to 20 kg and other animal products such as honey up to 2 kg. Non-animal foods are allowed in luggage, with import controls for products listed in Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 above 5 kg per fresh product and 2 kg per other product. The UK, apart from Northern Ireland, counts as a third country.
sources: https://www.fsai.ie/enforcement-and-legislation/legislation/food-legislation/imports/personal-imports
Food Safety Authority of Ireland — Personal imports of food from third countries
faq: Can I bring meat or cheese into Ireland from the UK or the USA?
No. The FSAI says meat and milk products are not allowed from third countries, which include the UK (not Northern Ireland), except up to 10 kg combined from the Faroe Islands or Greenland.
How much fish, honey and infant milk can I bring into Ireland?
Fish and shellfish up to 20 kg (or the weight of one fish if higher), other animal products such as honey up to 2 kg, and powdered infant milk or special medical food up to 2 kg combined.
Can I bring fruit, vegetables and nuts into Ireland?

They are allowed in luggage. Products listed in Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 are subject to import controls unless within 5 kg per fresh product and 2 kg per other product; products not on that list have no weight limit.
Do the rules apply to food from other EU countries?
No. The FSAI says the animal-product rules do not apply to products moved between EU Member States, or from Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino or Switzerland.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat and milk products are not allowed from third countries, the UK included.

lines: Meat and milk products are not allowed from third countries; the only exception is up to 10 kg combined from the Faroe Islands or Greenland.
The UK, other than Northern Ireland, counts as a third country. The rule does not apply to products from EU states, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino or Switzerland.

topics.label: Fish & honey
topics.head: Fish up to 20 kg and other animal products such as honey up to 2 kg.

lines: Fish and shellfish, such as prawns, lobsters and eviscerated fish: 20 kg, or the weight of one fish if higher; no limit from the Faroe Islands or Greenland.
Other animal products, such as honey, live oysters and snails: maximum 2 kg for personal use (10 kg combined from the Faroe Islands or Greenland).

topics.label: Baby & medical food
topics.head: Powdered infant milk and special medical food are allowed up to 2 kg combined.

lines: Powdered infant milk, other infant formula and special foods for medical reasons: up to 2 kg combined, sealed and branded, needing no refrigeration before opening.
They must be in luggage, not sent by post. Special medical pet food has the same 2 kg limit.

topics.label: Fruit, veg & nuts
topics.head: Allowed in luggage, with limits on products under EU import controls.

lines: Fruit, vegetables, nuts, cereals, tea and spices are allowed in luggage.

Products listed in Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 are subject to import controls unless within 5 kg per fresh product and 2 kg per other product. The limits apply per product; products not on the list have no weight limit.

topics.label: If it does not comply
topics.head: Food that does not meet the rules is treated as an import.

lines: If food does not meet these criteria it is subject to official controls and you are treated as an official importer.
For large quantities the page points to Revenue and Customs (ecustoms@revenue.ie). It does not describe penalties or a declaration procedure.

Switzerland.answer: Switzerland's customs authority (BAZG) says ready-to-eat food and soft drinks for the travel day can be brought in duty-free. It states that taking meat and dairy products, and most fruit and many vegetables, from non-EU countries into Switzerland is prohibited, and refers to the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (BLV) for details. VAT applies to other goods above a total value of CHF 150.
sources: https://www.bazg.admin.ch/de/allgemeine-informationen-zu-freimengen-und-wertfreigrenzen
Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (BAZG) — General information on duty-free quantities and value limits
faq: Can I bring a sandwich or snack into Switzerland?
Yes: BAZG says ready-to-eat food and non-alcoholic drinks for the travel day can be brought in duty-free.
Can I bring meat or cheese into Switzerland from a non-EU country?
No. BAZG says taking meat and dairy products, and most fruit and many vegetables, from non-EU countries is prohibited.
Where do I find the detailed rules for food?
BAZG refers to the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (BLV) for details, and to a separate page for food, alcohol and tobacco quantities.
When does VAT apply?
For other goods, VAT is due from a total value of CHF 150.

topics.label: Travel-day food
topics.head: Ready-to-eat food and soft drinks for the travel day come in duty-free.

lines: Ready-to-eat foods and non-alcoholic drinks for the travel day can be brought in duty-free.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat and dairy products from non-EU countries are prohibited.

lines: Taking meat and dairy products from third countries (non-EU states) into Switzerland is prohibited.
For details the page refers to the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (BLV).

topics.label: Fruit & veg
topics.head: Most fruit and many vegetables from non-EU countries are prohibited.

lines: Taking most fruit and many vegetables from third countries into Switzerland is prohibited.
The page gives no list of exceptions; BLV has the details.

topics.label: Limits & VAT
topics.head: VAT applies to other goods above a total value of CHF 150.

lines: For other goods VAT is due from a total value of CHF 150.
The page does not give exact quantity limits for food; it points to a sub-page on food, alcohol and tobacco quantities that we did not read.

Netherlands.answer: The Dutch government says that from outside the EU there are strict requirements for animal products and food, and you will almost always need a health certificate from the authorities of the country where the products are bought. The certificate states the product, weight, country of origin and EU destination country. From other EU countries you may bring animal products such as meat or dairy for your own use. Dutch Customs keeps a list of animal products that do not need a certificate.
sources: https://www.government.nl/topics/travelling-outside-the-netherlands/customs-declarations/transport-of-animal-products-to-the-netherlands
Government of the Netherlands — Transport of animal products to the Netherlands
faq: Can I bring meat or cheese into the Netherlands from outside the EU?
You will almost always need a health certificate. The Dutch government says there are strict requirements, with a few exceptions listed on the Dutch Customs website.
Can I bring meat or cheese from another EU country?
Yes, if it is for your own use. If you want to resell it or do not use it yourself, the conditions for the import of animal products apply.
What must the health certificate say?
The type of product, its weight, its country of origin and the EU country of destination. You get it from the authorities in the country where you buy the products.
Do protected species need permits?
Yes. You may not bring CITES-protected species or their products from outside the EU without the right permits, and some products, such as elephant ivory, are banned entirely.

topics.label: From other EU countries
topics.head: Meat and dairy from other EU countries are fine for your own use.

lines: You may bring animal products such as meat or dairy from other EU countries if you want to use them yourself.
If you want to resell them or do not plan to use them yourself, the conditions for the import of animal products apply.

topics.label: From outside the EU
topics.head: Strict requirements: you will almost always need a health certificate.

lines: The Dutch government says there are strict requirements for animal products and food from outside the EU, and as a general rule you need a health certificate.
Apply for it from the authorities in the country where the products are bought; the Dutch embassy there can tell you who to contact.
The type of product, its weight, its country of origin and the EU country of destination.
Dutch Customs (douane.nl) lists the animal products that do not need a health certificate; we did not read that list.

topics.label: Protected species
topics.head: CITES-protected species and their products need permits; some are banned.

lines: You may not bring endangered species protected by the CITES Convention, or their parts and products, from outside the EU without the correct permits.
Some products are banned entirely, such as elephant ivory. For the most endangered species you need CITES EU certificates; check the RVO website.

topics.label: Not read
topics.head: The page gives no weight limits or penalties.

lines: The page does not list exact weight or quantity limits, fruit and vegetable rules, honey, or penalties for breaking the rules.
Check Dutch Customs (douane.nl) before you bring food from outside the EU.

Spain.answer: Spain's tax agency says meat, meat products, milk and dairy products are banned from non-EU countries, with small exceptions: up to 2 kg combined of infant milk, baby food and medically required food, up to 2 kg of other animal products, and up to 20 kg of fish. Animal products from Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland and Great Britain are not subject to the restrictions. Ceuta and Melilla are outside the EU customs territory, so national rules apply there.
sources: https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es/Sede/viajeros-trabajadores-desplazados-fronterizos/viajeros/alimentos-origen-animal.html
Agencia Tributaria (Spanish Tax Agency) — Foods of animal origin for travellers
faq: Can I bring ham or cheese into Spain from outside the EU?

No: the agency says meat, meat products, milk and dairy products are banned, apart from the exceptions listed. Animal products from Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland and Great Britain are not subject to these restrictions.
How much fish can I bring into Spain?
Fresh eviscerated, prepared or processed fish: 20 kg combined or, if more than 20 kg, the weight of one fish. From the Faroe Islands or Greenland, fish products are exempt.
What about baby milk and pet food?

Infant milk, baby food, medically necessary special foods and pet food needed for health reasons: 2 kg combined, branded, retail-packaged and intact, needing no refrigeration. The pet food must be for the accompanying pet.
Do the rules apply to Ceuta and Melilla?
They are outside the EU customs territory, so national rules apply. The agency points to the Ministry of Health or the territorial services in both cities.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat, meat products, milk and dairy are banned from non-EU countries.

lines: The introduction of meat and meat products, milk and dairy products is prohibited, with the exceptions below.
Items that qualify under the exceptions are exempt from official controls at border posts.

scen.when: From Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, Great Britain
lines: Animal products from these places are not subject to the restrictions.
Shipments between EU member states are not subject to them either.

topics.label: Fish
topics.head: Fresh eviscerated, prepared or processed fish: 20 kg combined.

lines: 20 kg combined, or, if more than 20 kg, the weight of one fish.
Fish products from the Faroe Islands or Greenland are exempt; the page gives no weight limit for them.

topics.label: Baby, medical & pet food
topics.head: 2 kg combined for infant milk, baby food, medical foods and health-related pet food.

lines: Infant milk, infant food and medically necessary special foods: 2 kg combined, branded, retail-packaged, in an intact package unless already being consumed, and needing no refrigeration before opening.
Pet food needed for health reasons: within the same 2 kg, for the accompanying pet, long-life, branded and in an intact package.

topics.label: Other animal products
topics.head: Other animal goods not in the banned list are limited to 2 kg combined.

lines: Other goods not covered above and not listed in Part 2 of Annex I of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2122: 2 kg combined.
From the Faroe Islands or Greenland, other goods (not plants for planting or fish products): 10 kg combined.
They are outside the EU customs territory, so national rules apply; check the Ministry of Health or the territorial Agriculture, Fisheries and Border Health services in each city.

topics.label: Not read
topics.head: The page does not cover honey, eggs, penalties or where to declare.

lines: The page does not mention honey or eggs, penalties, or where to declare at customs, and says nothing about fruit and vegetables.
It gives African swine fever, avian flu and Ebola as reasons for the controls.

Finland.answer: The Finnish Food Authority says food cannot be freely imported into Finland from outside the EU, and online orders follow the same rules. From outside the EU, meat, meat products, milk, dairy and fresh fruit and vegetables without a phytosanitary certificate are prohibited. Allowed in small amounts: up to 2 kg of infant formula and medical food, 20 kg of fish and up to 2 kg of other animal products such as honey and eggs. Processed plant foods such as coffee, tea, nuts and canned fruit come in freely.
sources: https://www.ruokavirasto.fi/en/foodstuffs/instructions-for-consumers/bringing-food-for-private-use/
Ruokavirasto (Finnish Food Authority) — Bringing food for private use
faq: Can I bring meat or cheese into Finland from outside the EU?

No. The Finnish Food Authority lists meat and meat products, milk and dairy products as prohibited from outside the EU. Norway, Iceland and Switzerland follow the same rules as EU member states for animal-origin food.
How much fish and honey can I bring into Finland?
Fish, shellfish and roe: 20 kg in total, or one gutted fish. Other animal-origin products such as honey, frog legs, snails and eggs: up to 2 kg.
Can I bring fruit and vegetables into Finland?

Fresh produce from outside the EU needs a phytosanitary certificate, which the page says is difficult for travellers to obtain; this also applies to Norway and Iceland. Processed plant foods such as canned fruit and vegetables, nuts, coffee, tea and spices are allowed freely.
What if I bring a banned product by mistake?
The page says to dispose of the product and its scraps thoroughly as mixed waste.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat and milk products from outside the EU are prohibited.

lines: Meat and meat products, milk and dairy products are prohibited; online orders and mail follow the same rules.
Norway, Iceland and Switzerland: animal-origin foods follow the same rules as EU member states.

Food can generally be brought in, but pork and wild boar products from areas with African swine fever, which the page says includes Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and many other European countries, are allowed only with the oval EU identification mark on the package.
The Food Authority recommends not importing pork or wild boar products from ASF countries, and a wild boar caught on a hunting trip cannot be brought in from ASF areas.

topics.label: Fish & honey
topics.head: Fish up to 20 kg; honey, eggs, snails and frog legs up to 2 kg.

lines: Fish, shellfish and roe, fresh or processed: 20 kg in total, or one gutted fish.
Other animal-origin products, including honey, frog legs, snails and eggs: up to 2 kg.
Infant formula, baby food and foods for specific medical reasons: up to 2 kg.

topics.label: Fruit & veg
topics.head: Fresh produce from outside the EU needs a phytosanitary certificate.

lines: Fresh fruit, berries, vegetables and root vegetables from outside the EU need a phytosanitary certificate, which is hard for travellers to get. This also applies to Norway and Iceland.
Fruit and vegetables from Switzerland can be imported without restrictions; fruit and vegetables from the Canary Islands need a certificate.
Processed plant foods such as coffee, tea, spices, dried herbs, canned fruit and vegetables, nuts, seeds and flour.
Pineapples, bananas, durians, coconuts and dates; edible mushrooms up to 10 kg.

topics.label: Other foods
topics.head: Any food without fresh or processed meat or milk can be brought in.

lines: Any other food that contains no fresh or processed meat or milk.

Fish-stuffed olives, coffee, tea or maté extracts, coffee substitutes, miso and soy sauce with a little fish stock, packaged soup stocks and flavourings, packaged supplements with processed animal products (glucosamine, chondroitin, chitosan), and liqueurs and cordials.
The page does not cover pet food, frozen foods, confectionery beyond the general rules, or penalties for violations.

Sweden.answer: The Swedish Board of Agriculture says you may bring any food for personal use from other EU countries, and from Northern Ireland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Animal-origin products are allowed from San Marino, Andorra, Iceland, Norway, the Faroe Islands and Greenland (10 kg cap for the last two), but most animal products from other non-EU countries are prohibited, apart from up to 2 kg of honey, eggs and similar items, up to 2 kg of infant milk and medical food, and up to 20 kg of fish. You are responsible for checking that your product falls under an exception.
sources: https://jordbruksverket.se/languages/english/swedish-board-of-agriculture/food-and-beverages/bringing-in-or-ordering-food-and-drinks-to-sweden-as-a-private-individual
Jordbruksverket (Swedish Board of Agriculture) — Bringing in or ordering food and drinks to Sweden as a private individual
faq: Can I bring any food from another EU country to Sweden?
Yes, for personal use. Fresh plants from the Canary Islands, Ceuta, Melilla and some French overseas territories count as non-EU for plant health.
Can I bring meat or milk from outside the EU into Sweden?

Mostly prohibited. Allowed from San Marino, Andorra, Iceland, Norway, the Faroe Islands and Greenland (10 kg total for the last two). Shelf-stable products without meat such as chocolate, pasta, bread and biscuits are also allowed.
How much honey, eggs and fish can I bring from a non-EU country?

Up to 2 kg of honey, insects, eggs, snails, live oysters, frog legs and similar products, and up to 20 kg (or the weight of one fish, whichever is higher) of eviscerated fresh, prepared or processed fishery products.
What happens if Customs stops my food?

Stopped products are returned to the sender or destroyed, and Customs decides which. The page describes no fines. If you are unsure, do not bring the product: the Board does not answer questions about individual products.

topics.label: From EU countries
topics.head: Any food for personal use is allowed from other EU countries.

lines: You may bring any type of food product for personal use from EU Member States.
Fresh plants from the Canary Islands, Ceuta, Melilla and several French overseas territories follow non-EU plant rules.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: From most non-EU countries animal products are prohibited.

lines: All food types: Northern Ireland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
Animal-origin products such as milk, eggs and meat: San Marino, Andorra, Iceland, Norway, the Faroe Islands and Greenland.
The Faroe Islands and Greenland have a limit of 10 kg of animal products in total, and customs charges may apply.
Most animal-origin products are prohibited.

Exceptions: shelf-stable foods without meat such as chocolate, sweets, pasta, cereals, bread and biscuits, coffee and tea extracts and liqueur; they must meet Article 3.1 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/630.

topics.label: Honey, fish & baby food
topics.head: 2 kg of honey and similar, 2 kg of infant milk, 20 kg of fish.

lines: Up to 2 kg of honey, insects, eggs, snails, live oysters, frog legs and other products not otherwise prohibited.
Up to 2 kg of powdered infant milk, infant formula and special medical food, unopened, branded, needing no refrigeration and for your own use.
Up to 20 kg, or the weight of one fish if higher, of eviscerated fresh, prepared or processed fishery products.

topics.label: Fruit, veg & plants
topics.head: Fresh produce from outside the EU generally needs a phytosanitary certificate.

lines: Fresh fruit, vegetables, herbs and living plant parts generally need a phytosanitary certificate, except from Northern Ireland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
No certificate for fresh pineapple, banana, dates, durian or coconut, or for dried, frozen or processed products such as coffee, tea, spices, juice, jam or flour.
Some plants are banned outright, including potatoes and grape leaves.

topics.label: If it is stopped
topics.head: Customs returns or destroys stopped products; you must check the exceptions yourself.

lines: Swedish Customs stops prohibited products and products over a weight limit, and returns them to the sender or destroys them.

You are responsible for ensuring the product is covered by the exceptions; the Board does not answer questions about individual products, and if you are unsure you should not bring it in. The page describes no fines.

Austria.answer: Austrian Customs says imports of meat, dairy and other animal products, including in transit, are subject to official checks to prevent animal diseases from entering the EU, and that personal-use amounts are limited by a separate veterinary rules document. Because African swine fever cases have been found near Austria's borders, it asks travellers not to bring meat products, especially pork or wild boar from private production or home slaughter. Importing more than the personal-use amount needs certificates and is possible only at certain customs offices.
sources: https://www.bmf.gv.at/themen/zoll/reise/einfuhrverbote-einfuhrbeschraenkungen/mengenbegrenzungen-lebensmittel.html
Austrian Federal Ministry of Finance (Zoll) — Meat, dairy and other animal products: quantity limits
faq: Can I bring meat products into Austria?

Austrian Customs says to avoid it: travellers are asked not to bring meat or meat products, especially pork or wild boar products from private production or home slaughter, because African swine fever cases have been recorded near the border.
Are there quantity limits for animal products?
Yes. The page says limits apply and refers to a separate veterinary rules document listing the amounts that need no official control; we could not read the exact figures.
Can I bring larger quantities?
Only with the proper certificates, and only through certain customs offices that carry out the official control.
Can import bans change suddenly?
Yes. If an animal disease breaks out in your holiday country, authorities can impose import bans at short notice.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Quantities are limited; do not bring pork or wild boar from private production.

lines: Imports of meat, meat products, milk, dairy and other animal products, including transit, are subject to official checks to prevent animal diseases from entering the EU.
The page says quantity limits apply and refers to a separate PDF (Veterinärbestimmungen für Waren tierischen Ursprungs für den persönlichen Verbrauch), whose exact kg values we could not read.
More than the personal-use amount needs the right certificates, and the import is possible only at customs offices that carry out the official control.

topics.label: African swine fever
topics.head: Austrian Customs asks you not to bring meat from private production.

lines: Cases of African swine fever have been recorded near Austria’s borders, and Customs is checking more intensively.
Travellers are asked not to bring meat or meat products, especially pork or wild boar from private production or home slaughter.
Do not dispose of food scraps carelessly; the page recommends buying from approved Austrian retailers or controlled farm-gate sellers.

topics.label: Sudden import bans
topics.head: Authorities can impose import bans at short notice after an outbreak.

lines: If an animal disease breaks out in your holiday country, import bans can be imposed at short notice.
Wildlife and species protection rules may also apply.

topics.label: Not read
topics.head: The page gives no kg figures, exempt countries or penalties.

lines: The page does not mention fish, exempt countries or penalties, and does not give kg figures; the separate PDF it refers to was not readable here.
Check the Zoll travel pages or the customs hotline before you travel with animal products.

Czechia.answer: The Czech Customs Administration says that, under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2122, it is prohibited to import consignments of meat and milk products into the Union. Personal-consumption imports are allowed only from Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino and Switzerland, and from the Faeroe Islands and Greenland in limited quantities of up to 10 kg per person.
sources: https://celnisprava.gov.cz/en/dalsi-kompetence/informace-pro-fyzicke-osoby/Pages/veterinary-goods.aspx
Czech Customs Administration — Veterinary goods (personal consumption imports)
faq: Can I bring meat or milk products into Czechia from a non-EU country?

No. The customs page says it is prohibited to import meat and milk products into the Union, with personal-consumption imports allowed only from Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino and Switzerland.
Is anything allowed from the Faeroe Islands or Greenland?
Yes, in limited quantities of up to 10 kg per person.
Where do I find the rules on baby food, fish and penalties?
The page does not cover infant food, fish or penalties; it directs readers to the customs helpdesk and contact centre listed on the site.
Which regulation applies?
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2122, as cited by the Czech Customs Administration.

topics.label: Meat & milk
topics.head: Meat and milk products cannot be imported from outside the EU.

lines: It is prohibited to import in the Union any consignments of meat and milk products, under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2122.

scen.when: From Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland
lines: Personal-consumption imports are allowed from these six places.

scen.when: From the Faeroe Islands and Greenland
lines: Allowed in limited quantities, up to 10 kg per person.

topics.label: Not read
topics.head: The page does not cover baby food, fish, fruit, vegetables, penalties or how to declare.

lines: The page does not mention infant food, fish, penalties or how to declare these goods, and nothing on fruit, vegetables or plants.
It directs readers to the customs helpdesk and the contact centre listed on its site.

Chile.answer: Chile's Agricultural and Livestock Service (SAG) says everyone entering Chile, Chilean or foreign, must declare under oath every plant or animal product they carry in clothing, luggage or transport, whatever the quantity and however long ago they got it. A SAG inspector then decides whether each item may enter. You file the digital sworn declaration at Santiago airport or at land border controls.
sources: https://www.sag.gob.cl/ambitos-de-accion/ingreso-chile
SAG (Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero) — Entering Chile: sworn declaration
faq: Do I have to declare food when entering Chile?

Yes. SAG says everyone entering Chile must declare, individually and under oath, the plant and animal products they carry, regardless of quantity or how long ago they obtained them. Only commercial cargo is exempt from this declaration.
Who decides whether my food can enter Chile?
A SAG inspector evaluates each declared item. Declaring does not by itself mean the product is allowed.
Where do I file the declaration?
The digital sworn declaration (Declaración Jurada Digital) is filed at Arturo Merino Benítez Airport (SCL) or at land border controls.
What if I am not sure whether something needs declaring?
Ask a SAG inspector before submitting, call +56 2 2345 1100, or use the SAG contact form.

topics.label: Declare everything
topics.head: Declare every plant or animal product under oath, whatever the quantity.

lines: Everyone entering, including Chileans, foreigners, diplomats and officials, declares individually under oath on the sworn declaration form.
It covers plant and animal products, parts and by-products in your clothing, luggage or transport, unless the goods are commercial cargo.

topics.label: How to declare
topics.head: File the digital declaration, then hand declared items to the SAG inspector.

lines: File the Declaración Jurada Digital at Arturo Merino Benítez Airport (SCL) or at land border controls.
Hand over declared items for inspection; the SAG inspector decides whether each may enter. Vehicles and other transport are inspected after migration and customs control.
Ask an SAG inspector before submitting, call +56 2 2345 1100, or use the SAG contact form.

topics.label: Why it matters
topics.head: Undeclared products could harm national production and export markets.

lines: SAG says undeclared products could harm national production, possibly requiring eradication or control plans, causing major economic losses and reducing the trust of export markets.

topics.label: Not read
topics.head: The page lists no prohibited foods and gives no fine amounts.

lines: This page does not list prohibited items such as fruit, meat or dairy, and gives no fine amounts. Ask SAG at +56 2 2345 1100 before you bring any of them.

Thailand.answer: Suvarnabhumi Airport's plant import guide, based on Thailand's plant quarantine rules, says fresh fruits from all countries are banned, as are seeds and cuttings, soil, organic fertiliser and animal pests. Fresh vegetables, ornamental plants, seeds and grains, dried tea leaves, fresh coffee beans and mushrooms may come in only if declared to a plant quarantine officer with a phytosanitary certificate. Violations can mean up to one year in prison or a fine of up to 20,000 THB.
sources: https://suvarnabhumi.airportthai.co.th/service/airport-guide/detail/ProhibitedPlantforImport
Suvarnabhumi Airport (Airports of Thailand) — Prohibited plants for import
faq: Can I bring fresh fruit into Thailand?
The airport guide lists fresh fruits from all countries as banned, with kiwi, orange and banana as examples. Some frozen fruit is exempt, for example frozen kiwi below -17.8°C from any country.
Can I bring vegetables, tea or coffee into Thailand?

Fresh vegetables, ornamental plants, seeds or grains, dried tea leaves, fresh coffee beans and mushrooms may be brought if declared to a plant quarantine officer with a phytosanitary certificate and found free from pests and disease.
What is the penalty?
Under Section 21, imprisonment for up to one year or a fine of up to 20,000 THB, or both.
Which documents are needed for plant imports?
Form P.Q.5 (declaration), P.Q. 2-1 (permit for prohibited articles), a controlled seed licence if applicable, a CITES permit if applicable, and a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin.

topics.label: Fresh fruit
topics.head: Fresh fruits from all countries are banned.

lines: Fresh fruits from all countries are banned, including kiwi, orange and banana.
Some frozen fruit is exempt: for example frozen kiwi at a temperature below -17.8°C is allowed from any country.

topics.label: Veg, tea & coffee
topics.head: Allowed only if declared with a phytosanitary certificate.

lines: Fresh vegetables, ornamental plants, seeds or grains, dried tea leaves, fresh coffee beans and mushrooms may be brought in if declared to a plant quarantine officer, with a phytosanitary certificate, and found free from pests and diseases.

topics.label: Seeds, soil & plants
topics.head: Seeds, cuttings, soil, organic fertiliser and animal pests are prohibited.

lines: Propagating materials such as seeds and cuttings, soil, organic fertiliser and animal pests are on the prohibited list.
Restricted plants such as mango, apple, grape and some seeds are listed in a table with approved origin countries and required documents.

topics.label: Documents & fines
topics.head: Violations can mean up to one year in prison or a 20,000 THB fine.

lines: Form P.Q.5 (declaration), P.Q. 2-1 (permit for prohibited articles), P.P.5 (controlled seed licence), a CITES permit where it applies, and a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin.
Section 21: imprisonment for up to one year or a fine of up to 20,000 THB, or both.
This airport page covers plants only; it does not cover meat, dairy or fish. Ask the Department of Livestock Development before you bring animal products.

Croatia.answer: Croatia's Ministry of Agriculture says that if you arrive from a non-EU country the import of most products of animal origin is prohibited, and meat, milk and their products are not allowed from third countries other than the Faroe Islands, Greenland and Iceland, where up to 10 kg per person is allowed. Small amounts are allowed: 2 kg of infant milk, medical food and other animal products such as honey and eggs, and 20 kg of fish. Products over the limits are confiscated and destroyed at the traveller's cost, and undeclared ones can bring a fine.
sources: https://Inspektorat.gov.hr/UserDocsImages//ustrojstvo/9-sektor-za-veterinarski-nadzor-i-nadzor-sigurnosti-hrane-140/granicna-veterinarska-inspekcija//Brochure EN - products of animal origin in personal luggage.pdf
Croatian Ministry of Agriculture (Border Veterinary Inspection) — Which products can I import into the Republic of Croatia
faq: Can I bring meat or milk into Croatia from a non-EU country?
No. The brochure says import of meat, milk and products derived from them is not allowed from third countries, except up to 10 kg per person in total from the Faroe Islands, Greenland or Iceland.
Does it matter where the product was made?

Yes. What counts is the country you enter from, not where the product was packaged or made. A product labelled as made in the EU but brought in from a third country is treated as a third-country product.
How much fish, honey and eggs can I bring?

Fish: 20 kg or the weight of one fish per person, whichever is larger, with fresh fish gutted. Honey, eggs, egg products, live shellfish, snail meat and frog legs: 2 kg per person (10 kg from the Faroe Islands, Greenland or Iceland).
What happens to excess or banned products?
They are confiscated and destroyed, and the traveller bears all costs of safe destruction. If you fail to declare them you may be fined or judicial proceedings may be started.

topics.label: Meat & milk
topics.head: Meat, milk and their products from third countries are not allowed.

What counts is the country you enter from, not where the product was made or packaged.

lines: Milk, meat and other animal products are not restricted in personal luggage.

lines: Fresh fish must be gutted. Includes dried, cooked, marinated or smoked fish and some shellfish such as prawns, lobsters, mussels and oysters.
No restrictions on fishery products from the Faroe Islands or Iceland. Caviar of sturgeon: up to 125 g per person, more needs CITES papers.

topics.label: Honey, eggs & baby food
topics.head: 2 kg of honey, eggs, shellfish and similar; 2 kg of medical baby milk and food.

lines: Honey, eggs, egg products, live shellfish, snail meat and frog legs: up to 2 kg per person (10 kg from the Faroe Islands, Greenland or Iceland).
Powdered infant milk, infant food and special foods used only for medical purposes: up to 2 kg, in unopened proprietary-brand packaging that needs no refrigeration; home-made products do not qualify.
Raw eggs for humans are not allowed from South Korea, China and Malaysia, and raw honeycomb is not allowed.

topics.label: No limit
topics.head: Bread, biscuits, chocolate and pasta need no restriction.

lines: Bread, cakes (except with visible meat or milk added after cooking), cookies, chocolate and confectionery (except some Asian sweets high in unprocessed dairy).

Packaged food supplements, meat extracts, olives stuffed with fish, pasta without meat filling, stocks and flavourings, and other room-temperature foods without meat or unprocessed dairy and with less than 50% processed egg or fish.

topics.label: Excess & penalties
topics.head: Over the limits means confiscation, destruction at your cost, and possibly a fine.

lines: Products above the limits, or from a country where import is not allowed, are confiscated and destroyed, and the traveller bears all costs.
Failing to declare them may bring a fine or judicial proceedings. Larger quantities must travel as commercial shipments with a veterinary certificate and be registered at a border inspection post.

Latvia.answer: Latvia's State Revenue Service says meat, dairy, potatoes and pet food with meat or milk are prohibited in personal baggage from non-EU countries, with allowed amounts of up to 2 kg of honey, eggs and similar items, up to 20 kg of fish and up to 5 kg of listed fresh non-animal products. Agricultural and animal feed products from Russia and Belarus are banned, and you can leave prohibited items in labelled bins before inspection to avoid an offence. Prohibited or excess products are confiscated and destroyed.
sources: https://www.vid.gov.lv/en/food-products
State Revenue Service of Latvia (VID) — Food products in travellers’ personal baggage
faq: Can I bring meat, cheese or milk into Latvia from a non-EU country?
No. VID lists meat and meat products, and milk and dairy products including cheese, butter, cream, yoghurt and ice-cream, as prohibited in personal baggage for private use.
Can I bring potatoes or pet food?
Potatoes are prohibited, and so is pet food containing meat or milk, and chewable dog toys.
What is the weight limit for fish and honey?
Up to 20 kg of fish products and up to 2 kg of animal-origin products such as honey and eggs, with no limit on fish from the Faroe Islands and Greenland.
Can I leave banned food at the border?
Yes: travellers are asked to leave prohibited products in special labelled containers at the customs control point before inspection, to avoid an administrative offence.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat, cheese, milk and meat-containing pet food are prohibited from non-EU countries.

lines: Meat and meat products, including poultry, sausages, canned meat, meat-filled pastry, gravy and soups.
Milk and dairy products, including cheese, butter, cream, yoghurt, kefir, condensed milk and ice-cream.
Pet food containing meat or milk, and chewable dog toys; potatoes; all dried beans originating in Nigeria.

scen.when: From Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland
lines: No quantity restrictions apply to animal-origin products for private use from these places.

topics.label: Allowed in small amounts
topics.head: Honey and eggs up to 2 kg, fish up to 20 kg, fresh produce up to 2 or 5 kg.

lines: Up to 2 kg of products such as honey, eggs, live oysters and shellfish, snails, royal jelly and bee glue, and baby milk powder, baby food, medical foods and certain pet food in patented packaging (10 kg from the Faroe Islands and Greenland).
Up to 20 kg of fresh (gutted), dried, heat-treated, salted, smoked or canned fish and some crustaceans; sturgeon roe up to 125 g per package with a special label; no products from Russia or Belarus.
Up to 2 kg of fruit, vegetables and nuts in shell if you hold a phytosanitary certificate from the third country; above 2 kg they must be presented to the Food and Veterinary Service.
Up to 5 kg of listed fresh non-animal products or 2 kg of other dried or prepared ones; wild berries and mushrooms up to 10 kg fresh.

topics.label: Allowed freely
topics.head: Bread, cakes, chocolate, pasta, bananas, dates and pineapples need no restriction.

lines: Processed non-animal foods such as bread, cakes, cookies, candy, chocolate and pasta.
Bananas, coconuts, dates, pineapples and durians, but not from Russia or Belarus.

topics.head: Agricultural and feed products from Russia and Belarus are prohibited.

lines: Agricultural and animal feed products from Russia and Belarus are prohibited; the page links to a PDF list.
Goods under EU sanctions from there, such as spirits, caviar and crustaceans, are prohibited too.

topics.head: Banned or excess products are confiscated and destroyed.

lines: Travellers from non-EU countries are subject to strict veterinary control at the border crossing; prohibited or excess products are confiscated and destroyed, and a repeated violation results in a penalty. The page gives no amounts.
To avoid an offence, leave prohibited products in the special labelled containers at the customs control point before inspection.

Belgium.answer: The Belgian food safety agency says travellers returning from a non-EU country should not bring meat, meat products, milk or dairy products for personal use in their luggage. Small amounts are allowed: up to 2 kg of powdered infant milk, baby food and medically required special food, up to 20 kg of fish, and up to 2 kg of other animal products such as honey, eggs and snails. The rules do not apply to products moved between EU states or from Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino or Switzerland.
sources: https://www.fasfc.be/node/497
FASFC (Belgian Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain) — travelling with food: meat, dairy and animal products
faq: Can I bring meat or cheese into Belgium from outside the EU?
FASFC says travellers returning from a non-EU country should not bring meat, meat products, milk or dairy products for personal use.
How much fish and honey can I bring into Belgium?
Fishery products up to 20 kg for personal consumption, or the weight of one fish if higher, and up to 2 kg of other animal products such as honey, eggs, live oysters, live mussels and snails.
What about baby milk and special foods?

Powdered infant milk, infant food and special foods or pet feed required for medical reasons are allowed up to 2 kg, if they need no refrigeration, are a packaged proprietary brand with intact packaging, and are for you or your accompanying pets.
Which places are exempt?
The rules do not apply to animal products moved between EU Member States, or to products from Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino or Switzerland.

topics.label: Meat & dairy
topics.head: Meat, meat products, milk and dairy from non-EU countries should not be brought in.

lines: Do not bring meat, meat products, milk or dairy products in your luggage for personal use.
The rules do not apply to animal products moved between EU Member States, or to products from Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino or Switzerland.

topics.label: Fish
topics.head: Up to 20 kg of fish for personal consumption, or one fish if heavier.

lines: Includes fish and certain shellfish such as dead prawns, lobsters, mussels and oysters.

lines: Powdered infant milk, infant food and special foods or pet feed required for medical reasons: up to 2 kg, needing no refrigeration, in packaged proprietary-brand products with intact packaging unless in use, and for the traveller or accompanying pets.
Up to 2 kg of other animal products such as honey, eggs, live oysters, live mussels and snails.
